title: Build the plan
teaches: Putting the course together for one household: a spending rate, a bridge, a yearly income target, Social Security timing, and a test against every stretch of US history

blocks.text: The first half of the course was about how much a pile of savings can pay out, and the second about how to take it out without handing more than necessary to the tax system. A real plan needs both at once, because they interact: taxes and health premiums are spending too, and the order of withdrawals changes how much is left to weather a bad decade.

This lesson builds one plan, step by step, for a couple who are both 50 and want to stop working. They have $1.3 million in 401(k)s and IRAs, $700,000 in a taxable brokerage account with a basis (what they paid for the shares, lesson 7) of about two thirds of its value, and $100,000 in Roth IRAs, all of it contributions. They spend $80,000 a year, not counting income tax and health premiums, which come on top. Their combined Social Security at 70 will be about $55,800 a year in today's money. None of these numbers is anyone's in particular; the method is the point.[^not-advice]

$80,000 is 3.8 percent of $2.1 million. Lesson 4 said that over 45 years the worst US starts could sustain about 3.3 to 3.5 percent, before tax and health premiums. That puts this couple near the edge, and a little above it once taxes and premiums are added to what the portfolio has to pay.

Two things help. Social Security will cover about 70 percent of their spending from 70, so the portfolio pays for everything for only twenty years, and after that only the other 30 percent. And they can bend: in the spirit of lesson 5's guardrails, they write down now a rule they will follow: spending drops to $70,000 if the portfolio falls more than a quarter in real terms in the first decade.

parts.title: Step 2: the bridge and the brackets

blocks.text: From 50 to 60 they need about $80,000 a year without touching pre-tax money, which lesson 9 says calls for a taxable account, Roth contributions and a conversion ladder.[^sepp-alternative] The $700,000 taxable account covers the first years on its own; $100,000 of Roth contributions is a reserve. Meanwhile each year they convert pre-tax money to Roth, so that rungs ripen from 55 onwards.

How much to convert is set by health insurance until 65 (lesson 11). A couple of 50 to 64 with a benchmark plan around $24,000 a year has a strong reason to keep MAGI, the income the marketplace counts, under $84,600, the 400 percent cliff. Dividends of about 2 percent on the taxable account come to about $14,000, and selling $80,000 of shares with a third of it gain adds about $27,000, so roughly half the room is used before any conversion. The conversions are modest, perhaps $10,000 to $40,000 a year. From 65 to 70, with Medicare and before Social Security, they convert hard: to the top of the 12 percent bracket, $133,000 of income once the $32,200 standard deduction is added to the bracket's $100,800, minding Medicare's income surcharge, IRMAA, which looks back two years, so this year's income sets the premium two years on (lessons 10 and 12).

Their future benefit is mostly fixed already, though not yet paid: lesson 13's formula adds little for a high earner's last years of work, so stopping at 50 lowers it only a little. The higher earner waits to 70, which protects whichever of them lives longer; the years from 65 to 70 are the conversion window. After 70, the torpedo from lesson 12 makes further conversions dearer, and required withdrawals from 75 on what's left of the pre-tax accounts set the floor of their taxable income.

The figure runs the whole plan, taxes and premiums included, through every stretch of US returns long enough to reach 95, with 70 percent of the money in shares. The buttons above the figure choose how withdrawals are taken: the textbook order, filling the 12 percent bracket from the start, or staying under the ACA line until 65 and then filling 12 percent.

blocks.caption: The couple's combined balance, after inflation, from the age they stop work to 95, for every start year with enough history. Red lines ran short of the spending. Taxes, ACA premiums before 65, Medicare surcharges, conversions and Social Security at 70 are all included.
blocks.task: Find a spending level with no red lines, and one with some

blocks.text: At $80,000, under the ACA-aware plan, two starts run short, 1966 and 1973, in the couple's late eighties and nineties.[^starts-1966-1973] At $70,000 none does. Filling the 12 percent bracket from 50 leaves far less in a typical start, because it crosses the cliff in most years before 65: the couple loses the credit and pays the full premium, about $24,000 a year, more than the conversions save in later tax. The textbook order pays by far the most tax in dollars, yet ends with similar wealth in a typical start. Its tax is paid later, on pre-tax money that has grown for decades, so the bill is bigger, but it is much the same share of a bigger pile: tax deferred and paid later at the same rate costs nothing, which is lesson 8's rule again. The differences show up in the bad starts, and in how much of what is left at the end is still pre-tax money, on which heirs will owe income tax.

Now use the Stop work at slider: try 55 instead of 50. Five more years of saving and five fewer of spending move the plan from the edge to comfortable, a bigger change than switching between the three plans, the same lesson as the savings-rate curve in lesson 1: near the edge, a few years of work matter more than any tax trick.
A plan like this isn't set once. Each autumn, before the year's income is fixed:
**Check the spending rule.** Is the portfolio within the guardrails written down at the start? If not, cut or raise as planned.

**Estimate the year's income.** Dividends, gains already realised, any work. Then decide the year's conversion or gain harvesting against the right line: the ACA cliff before 65, the top of the 12 percent bracket, or the Medicare surcharge threshold two years on.
**Re-read the rules.** Brackets, the ACA percentages, IRMAA lines and contribution limits change every year, and sometimes the law does. This course's numbers are for 2026.

The optional branches pick up what the main lessons left out: Washington's own taxes and health programmes, Portugal for anyone thinking of living abroad, taxable-account tactics and estates, equity pay, couples, Medicare and care after 65, and other shapes of retirement, such as coasting or a paid-off house.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Taxes and health premiums are spending, so the withdrawal rate and the tax plan have to be tested together.
Before 65, the ACA line often sets how much to convert; from 65 to Social Security is the main conversion window.
Deferring tax costs nothing when the later rate equals the earlier one; the gains come from paying lower rates, not from paying later.
Near the edge, a few more years of work or a little less spending matter more than any tax strategy.

blocks.caption: Six questions on putting a plan together
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why should a withdrawal plan be tested with taxes and health premiums included?
choices: They are spending too, and the withdrawal order changes them
They are fixed amounts that don't change
items.why: A plan that spends $80,000 also pays tax and premiums from the portfolio, and how much depends on which accounts are drawn.

items.ask: For a couple of 50 to 64 on a marketplace plan, what often limits how much to convert each year?
choices: Keeping MAGI under the ACA cliff
items.why: Crossing 400 percent of the poverty line can cost the whole premium credit, often more than the conversion saves.

items.ask: Why are the years from 65 to 70 a good window for large conversions in this plan?
choices: Medicare has replaced the ACA credit, and Social Security hasn't started yet
items.why: Income no longer costs health credits, and there is no Social Security yet to trigger the torpedo.

items.ask: The textbook order paid far more lifetime tax but ended with similar wealth in a typical start. Why?
choices: Tax deferred and paid later at the same rate costs nothing
The textbook order earns higher returns
Heirs pay no tax on pre-tax accounts
items.why: As in lesson 8, deferral only helps or hurts through the difference between the rates.

items.ask: Why did filling the 12 percent bracket from 50 leave this couple less in a typical start?
choices: It gave up the ACA credit in most years before 65
It left the low brackets empty
items.why: The extra income each year pushed them over the cliff, costing about $24,000 a year in premiums.

items.ask: In the figure, what changed the plan most for a couple near the edge?
choices: Stopping work a few years later or spending a little less
Raising the money in shares from 70 to 75 percent
items.why: More years of saving and fewer of spending change the arithmetic of lesson 1 far more than tax tactics.

summary: **Test spending and tax together.** Taxes and premiums come out of the same portfolio and depend on which accounts are drawn.
**Start from a sustainable rate.** Over 45 years the worst US starts managed about 3.3 to 3.5 percent before tax.
**Bridge to 60 with taxable money and a ladder.** Convert each year so rungs ripen from five years after stopping.
**Let the ACA line set conversions before 65.** Then convert hard from 65 until Social Security.
**Delay the larger Social Security benefit to 70.** It protects the survivor and leaves the sixties for conversions.
**Deferral alone gains nothing.** The savings come from paying lower rates, not from paying later.
**Review every autumn.** The spending rule, the year's income target, and the year's rules.

not-advice.title: Rules, not personal advice
not-advice.text: This lesson teaches how the rules work and how they fit together; it is not personal financial or tax advice. Figures use 2026 federal rules.

sepp-alternative.title: When the taxable bridge is smaller
sepp-alternative.text: A household with almost everything in pre-tax accounts can instead tap them before 59½ without the 10 percent penalty through substantially equal periodic payments (section 72(t)), or from 55 from the 401(k) of the job they just left. Here the $700,000 taxable account is large enough that a simple conversion ladder does the job with more flexibility.

starts-1966-1973.title: 1966 and 1973
starts-1966-1973.text: Both starts ran into the stagflation of the 1970s, and as in lesson 3, losses in the first decade left too small a balance for the later boom to rebuild, so the money ran short decades later. A retiree in January 1966 saw the S&P 500 lose more than half its real value over the next nine years while consumer prices nearly doubled; a 1973 retiree took a 48 percent real stock drop in the very first two years.
